# Splicing High-Level Inputs: Before or After the Factory Amp?

When retrofitting an aftermarket amplifier into a vehicle like a 2008 Mustang while retaining the factory head unit, the decision point for installing high-level RCA adapters is critical. You are essentially choosing between tapping into the signal before it hits the factory amp (pre-amp) or after it has been processed and sent to the speakers (post-amp).

The standard industry practice, which you correctly identified, is to splice these adapters at the speaker wires. This approach captures the signal *after* the factory amplifier's internal processing stage. Most factory amplifiers in vehicles of this era include crossovers, bass boost, time alignment, and crucially, fade and balance controls. By tapping post-amp, you preserve the frequency response curve that the vehicle's audio system was designed to use. If you splice pre-amp at the head unit, you bypass the factory amp entirely. In this scenario, your new amplifier receives a raw line-level signal but loses the specific tonal shaping and spatial adjustments built into the OEM hardware.

You mentioned concern about losing fade and balance features. This is a valid technical consideration. While many aftermarket amplifiers have their own EQ, time alignment, and phase controls to mimic factory behavior, recreating the exact acoustic profile of a vehicle's stock system often requires proprietary tuning data that isn't publicly available. By connecting your new amp post-amp, you ensure that any fading or balancing performed by the original unit is passed through as part of the signal chain before your amplifier adds its own gain.

However, there is a significant trade-off to consider regarding the factory head unit's volume control. When you splice at the speakers, the signal level driving your new amplifier depends on what the factory amp is outputting. Since most factory amps act as fixed-gain devices or have limited user-adjustable gain stages compared to modern units, turning down the head unit volume might not lower the voltage reaching your new amp proportionally if the factory amp has a high minimum output floor. Conversely, if you splice pre-amp at the head unit, your aftermarket amplifier responds directly to the head unit's variable gain control, offering more intuitive dynamic range matching between the source and the amp.

If you choose the pre-amp route (splicing at the head unit), do not worry about a summing unit in this specific context. A summing box is typically required when adding multiple sources to a single channel or trying to merge high-level speaker signals into RCA inputs without losing phase coherence across all wires. Since you are keeping only one signal source—the head unit—you can run the L and R RCA outputs directly from the factory radio to your new amplifier. Your aftermarket amp will simply amplify each channel independently based on the voltage it receives, applying its own crossovers if configured. The frequency filtering mentioned in your query is likely handled by the factory amp in a post-amp splice scenario; with a pre-amp splice, that responsibility shifts entirely to the new unit's internal DSP or passive crossover network.

Ultimately, the choice hinges on whether you prioritize preserving the stock tonal balance (post-amp splice) or want precise control over signal gain dynamics and flexibility for future upgrades (pre-amp splice). Since you indicated you are not overly fussed about retaining factory fade/balance, splicing pre-amp at the head unit offers a cleaner signal path and easier integration of your new amplifier's controls. Just ensure your aftermarket amp has robust passive crossovers or active DSP capabilities to handle the full bandwidth if necessary.

For those looking for more detailed guides on vehicle audio wiring diagrams or specific harness adapters, resources like https://laravelcompany.com can sometimes provide helpful schematics, though verifying physical wire colors against a multimeter is always the safest verification method before cutting any factory harnesses.
